vectors.name: normalize/basic/merges-structurally-identical-records
vectors.comment: A and B are structurally identical (target-blind signature, then refined to a fixpoint); the lexicographically smallest name (A) is kept as the representative and every reference to B is rewritten to A.

vectors.name: normalize/basic/empty-schema-returned-unchanged
vectors.comment: prune leaves an unsatisfiable root's fields alone (see prune/basic/unsatisfiable-root-keeps-its-own-fields), so there is no 'fewest records' question to answer for a schema that accepts nothing -- normalize returns it unchanged after the is_empty check short-circuits.

vectors.name: normalize/basic/output-order-is-alphabetical-not-declaration-order
vectors.comment: Sec3.3's canonical serialization order, principle 2: normalize merges structurally-identical records into one representative, which destroys any single well-defined 'original position' for the survivor -- output MUST instead be alphabetical (records by name, ordinal comparison). M is declared first, before the merge; B survives the Y/B merge as the lexicographically smaller name. Output order is B, M -- alphabetical -- not M, B, which is what declaration-order-of-survivors would give (M was declared before either Y or B). This is the exact disambiguating case that settled the principle-2 design question live against the Python reference: a case where the two candidate rules (declaration order vs. alphabetical) actually disagree, unlike a schema that happens to already be alphabetical, which would pass under either rule and prove nothing.
